text.p: Britain on Friday blocked the proposed merger between brewing and hotel giant Bass Plc and Carlsberg-Tetley, confounding the market which had been expecting tough conditions for clearance -- not a thumbs down to the deal.

Margaret Beckett, the Labour government's new Trade and Industry Secretary, said in a statement she disagreed with the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) view that the negative effects of the merger could be dealt with by demanding the sale of 1,900 Bass pubs.
"I am not persuaded that the divestment of 1,900 pubs would be an adequate counterweight to the substantial strengthening of Bass's position as a producer and wholesaler of beer," she said.
Bass and Carlsberg were each in the process of drawing up a response but had no immediate comment to make.
The deal would have made Bass Britain's biggest brewer, handing it 35 percent of the domestic beer market.
Bass' existing market share is 23 percent, below Scottish and Newcastle Plc which makes 29 of every 100 pints consumed.
Taking the hardest line in her first major ruling on competition issues, Beckett said she was seeking an undertaking from Bass to sell its existing 50 percent stake in Carlsberg-Tetley.

The move marks a shift from past judgements on brewing mergers. Every acquisition in the beer industry since the Beer Orders Act of 1992 has required the merged group to reduce the size of its tied estate.

But Beckett said "Bass's acquisition of Carlsberg-Tetley would represent a further substantial step in the direction of concentration in an industry which has already seen a number of national brewers with tied estates fall from six to four since 1989."
This referred to the British brewing industry's tied pub system whereby pubs are only allowed to sell beer its own company has brewed.
The news was greeted with surprise in the market. Bass shares rose strongly, while Carlsberg shares fell in Copenhagen

Nick Lyle, brewing analyst at SocGen, said "I'm a bit taken aback. We had expected to see the deal to be tied to harsh conditions rather than completely blocked. It must be frustrating for Bass but it won't have lost a lot of cash on this."
Lyle estimated a net cash loss of 60 million pounds. However, Bass will receive proceeds from the forced sale of its Carlsberg-Tetley stake.
After months of recent uncertainty which had weighed on Bass shares, its shares rose to a high of 765 pence before settling for a 12 pence gain at 747.
"Carlsberg is not a great performer and people are saying it is a good thing Bass are out of it," said one dealer.
SocGen's Lyle added that it may also signal relief that the uncertainty about Bass' future had now been swept away.

But Carlsberg's shares suffered in the fallout, diving 19.1 crowns or 5.2 percent from Thursday's closing level of 365.1 -- the level at which is was suspended shortly before the British announcement.
Under the original terms of the deal, announced last August, Bass paid 200 million pounds for the 50 percent interest in Carlsberg-Tetley owned by drinks group Allied Domecq.

Carlsberg, the Danish brewer that held the rest, agreed to contribute its interest to Bass, together with 20 million pounds, in exchange for 20 percent of the merged Bass Brewers/Carlsberg-Tetley business.
Assessing the impact on jobs, observers had warned that while 2,500 jobs would have been lost if the deal had proceeded, twice as many might be lost if it was blocked.
